articles.title: FY2026 Patent Data Update: Grants, Publications, and Cross-Border Inventors
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch

This post updates my September 21, 2026 post on FY2026 utility grants that was projecting out to end of the FY. The year is now over. I have also added two new cuts of the data: published applications by origin and cross-border inventor teams.

The USPTO issued 315,825 utility patents in FY2026, down 3.8% from FY2025. About half of this drop is due to a calendar artifact -- FY2025 had 53 Tuesdays (the day patents issue) and FY2026 was back to the usual 52. But the weekly rate was down overall about 2%.

The two shifts in the mix that I reported in September held up. Continuing applications (continuations, divisionals, and CIPs) accounted for about 26% of FY2026 utility grants, down from 36% in FY2025. That is a major drop I discussed in prior posts.  Patents whose first-named inventor claims US residence fell below 40% for the first time.

articles.title: Ease Is Not Necessity: Third Circuit Affirms No Fair Use in Thomson Reuters v. ROSS
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch
The Third Circuit has affirmed partial summary judgment that ROSS Intelligence infringed Thomson Reuters's copyrights when it used Westlaw headnotes to train a competing AI legal search tool. Thomson Reuters Enterprise Centre GmbH v. ROSS Intelligence Inc., No. 25-2153 (3d Cir. Sept. 29, 2026).
Judge Bibas held as a matter of law that ROSS infringed 2,243 headnotes and that the copying was not fair use. He then certified two questions for immediate appeal: whether the headnotes are original, and whether ROSS's use was fair. The Third Circuit answered both for Thomson Reuters in an opinion by Judge Montgomery-Reeves. What remains for trial in Delaware is whether some of those copyrights have expired, the claims on the remaining headnotes, and damages. I previously wrote about Judge Bibas's decision (Feb. 11, 2025) and ROSS's opening brief on appeal (Sept. 23, 2025).
ROSS never showed a headnote to its users. The headnotes were copied and used to write AI training memos, and the finished tool returned only passages from judicial opinions. ROSS argued that this sort of intermediate copying is fair use under cases like Google LLC v. Oracle America, Inc., 593 U.S. 1 (2021). The court disagreed. In its reading, those cases turn on necessity, and ROSS already had the opinions and copied the headnotes because that was easier. "Unlike necessity, ease is not a justification for copying." The court called the dispute "no more than an ordinary copyright case" and set generative AI aside in a footnote responding to the Trump Administration's recent statement of interest in the OpenAI litigation.

articles.title: Clear but Impossible: Satius v. Samsung Moves Inoperable Claims from Indefiniteness to Enablement
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch
The Federal Circuit has affirmed invalidity of Satius's wireless-coupler patent, but on a different ground than the district court. Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., No. 2025-1446 (Fed. Cir. Oct. 1, 2026). Claim 1 of U.S. Patent No. 6,711,385 recites an apparatus "for transmitting electric or electromagnetic signals over air." Everyone agrees the first option is impossible: electromagnetic signals travel through air; electric signals do not. Magistrate Judge Burke (D. Del.) held the claims indefinite on that basis. Chief Judge Moore's opinion for the panel (joined by Judges Lourie and Hughes) rejects that reasoning, holding that a claim can be clear about its scope even when part of that scope is physically impossible. The court then held the claims invalid for lack of enablement, an issue the district court had found waived.
Judge Hughes previewed the result at oral argument: "If I claim the transporter from Star Trek, everybody knows what I'm claiming. It's impossible. But it's impossible because it's not enabled, not because it's indefinite." The panel's precedential opinion adopts that view.

articles.title: Method or Molecule: Judge Dyk Dissents from En Banc Denial in Teva v. Lilly
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch
The Federal Circuit has denied rehearing en banc in Teva v. Eli Lilly, leaving in place Judge Prost's April decision reinstating Teva's $177 million jury verdict against Lilly over its migraine drug Emgality. Teva Pharms. Int'l GmbH v. Eli Lilly & Co., 172 F.4th 1367 (Fed. Cir. 2026). Judge Dyk dissented, writing that the panel decision "creates confusion as to the enablement standards for method claims" and is contrary to Amgen Inc. v. Sanofi, 598 U.S. 594 (2023). In Amgen, the Supreme Court held that claims to an entire class of antibodies, defined only by their ability to bind a cholesterol-regulating protein called PCSK9 and block its activity, were not enabled.
The claims cover a method of "treating headache in a human" by administering "an effective amount of an anti-CGRP antagonist antibody" that is a "humanized monoclonal antibody." CGRP is a protein associated with migraine pain, and both Teva's Ajovy and Lilly's Emgality are antibodies that block it. The specification disclosed one humanized antibody within that genus (G1, Ajovy's active ingredient). It also described twelve mouse antibodies (shown in the figure above), which the panel viewed as just a routine humanization step away from the claimed genus. The panel assumed, for argument's sake, that making and humanizing every anti-CGRP antagonist antibody would take undue experimentation. Even with that assumption, it reversed the JMOL of non-enablement, reasoning that the claims recite only the use of the antibodies to treat headache, that anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies were already well known and humanizing them was routine, and that the specification taught that all of them treat headache.
Judge Dyk thought the method-versus-antibody distinction does no work: "Claiming a method of use that depends on a recited component cannot excuse the enablement requirement of the component."

articles.title: One Determination, Two Clocks: Crocs Asks the Supreme Court to Fix ITC Appeal Deadlines
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch
Crocs has asked the Supreme Court to decide when a single agency decision (by the ITC) becomes final for purposes of appeal. Crocs, Inc. v. International Trade Commission, No. 26-421. The underlying dispute is an ITC trademark fight over knock-off Classic Clogs, but the Federal Circuit never reached Crocs's loss against the three respondents who actually litigated (Hobby Lobby, Orly Shoe, and Amoji). Writing for the panel, Judge Stoll held that Crocs's appeal of that no-violation finding came 39 days late, even though Crocs filed within 60 days after the same Commission determination became final as to the exclusion order. Crocs, Inc. v. ITC, 163 F.4th 1374 (Fed. Cir. 2026). The full court denied rehearing en banc in April without noted dissent.
The question presented: Whether an agency disposition is final as to some issues, thus triggering deadlines for judicial review, while other issues decided in the same disposition remain subject to further executive or administrative review.
Crocs identifies a circuit split: the D.C. and Fourth Circuits treat an agency order as final all at once, while the Ninth Circuit and now the Federal Circuit allow issue-by-issue finality. The Solicitor General's response is due October 28. This is Crocs's second trip to the Court in about a year; its petition on "patented" as false advertising was denied in October 2025.
